questions.stem: A provider prescribes heparin 5,000 units subcutaneously. The vial is labeled 10,000 units per milliliter. How many milliliters should the nurse administer?

options.label: A
options.rationale: A quarter of a milliliter would deliver only 2,500 units, half the prescribed dose.

options.label: B
options.rationale: Desired dose divided by the concentration: 5,000 units divided by 10,000 units per milliliter equals 0.5 milliliter.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Two milliliters would deliver 20,000 units, four times the prescribed dose.

questions.teachingPoint: Dose calculations: desired dose divided by dose on hand, multiplied by the volume on hand. Always double-check high-alert drugs such as heparin.

questions.stem: Before administering digoxin to an adult client, the nurse notes an apical pulse of 54 beats per minute and a potassium level of 3.1 milliequivalents per liter. Which action should the nurse take?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Giving digoxin with bradycardia and hypokalemia raises the risk of toxicity and dangerous dysrhythmias.

options.label: B
options.text: Give half of the prescribed dose
options.rationale: Nurses may not alter a prescribed dose; the findings require holding the drug and contacting the provider.

options.label: C
options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider
options.rationale: An apical pulse below 60 and a low potassium level both increase the risk of digoxin toxicity, so the dose is held and the provider informed.

questions.teachingPoint: Hold digoxin for an apical pulse below 60 and watch potassium closely: hypokalemia potentiates digoxin toxicity.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after a transfusion of packed red blood cells begins, the client reports chills and low back pain and appears anxious. What is the nurse's first action?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop the transfusion and keep the vein open with normal saline through new tubing
options.rationale: Chills, back pain and anxiety early in a transfusion suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stopping the blood immediately limits the amount transfused.

options.label: B
options.text: Slow the transfusion rate and notify the provider
options.rationale: Slowing the infusion continues to deliver incompatible blood; the transfusion must be stopped entirely.

options.label: C
options.text: Administer acetaminophen and continue the transfusion
options.rationale: Treating symptoms while continuing the transfusion allows more incompatible blood to infuse and could be fatal.

questions.teachingPoint: For any suspected transfusion reaction: stop the blood, keep the line open with saline on new tubing, stay with the client, notify the provider and blood bank.
